name: Angkor Wat
summary: The largest religious monument on Earth — a 12th-century Khmer masterpiece rising from the jungle near Siem Reap.

practical.hours: Angkor Archaeological Park generally opens around sunrise; ticket booths and temple access hours vary by site — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: 1-, 3-, and 7-day Angkor Passes required. Buy only from official counters or the authorised online channel.
practical.dress: Cover shoulders and knees. Hats off inside shrine spaces. Comfortable shoes for uneven stone.
practical.duration: Half day for the main complex; multi-day for the wider park.

etiquette: Do not climb on restricted towers or bas-reliefs.
Keep voices low near active worship spaces.
Ask before photographing people at prayer.
Drones are restricted — check current park rules.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Fly into Siem Reap (SAI). Tuk-tuks and licensed guides are the usual way into the park; hire for the day rather than hopping ad hoc.
visitGuide.bestTime: November–February (cooler, drier). Sunrise at the reflecting pools is popular — arrive early and leave room for quieter mid-morning exploration.
notes: Verify opening hours and ticket rules before visit — they change seasonally.
Bring water, sun protection, and cash for small vendors.
Many towers have steep, uneven steps; skip if mobility is limited.

name: Borobudur
summary: A vast 9th-century Mahayana Buddhist stupa-temple — terraces of stone reliefs ascending toward a silent, misty summit.

practical.hours: Daytime access is standard; sunrise tickets are sold separately when offered — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Official Borobudur tickets via authorised operators; international and domestic rates differ.
practical.dress: Modest clothing. Temple cloth (sarong) may be required for upper levels — usually provided with entry.

etiquette: Walk clockwise on the galleries when following traditional practice.
Do not sit or stand on Buddha statues or stupas.
Follow staff directions on which tiers are open.
visitGuide.gettingThere: About 40–60 minutes from Yogyakarta by car. Organised tours and private drivers are common.
visitGuide.bestTime: Dry season (roughly April–October). Sunrise is atmospheric but crowded; mid-morning light is excellent for reliefs.
notes: Capacity limits may apply on upper terraces — book ahead when required.
Verify before visit: access rules have tightened in recent years.

name: Meiji Shrine
summary: A forest sanctuary in central Tokyo dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shōken — quiet paths, towering torii, living tradition.

practical.hours: Sunrise to sunset typically; exact times shift with the season — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Shrine grounds are free. Inner gardens and special exhibitions may have fees.
practical.dress: Modest, tidy attire. Remove hats when approaching the main hall.
practical.duration: 1–2 hours for paths, purification, and the main hall.

etiquette: Bow once before passing under a torii; walk to the side, not the centre path reserved for deities.
Purify hands and mouth at the temizuya before approaching.
At the hall: toss a coin, bow twice, clap twice, bow once (common practice — follow posted guidance).
No eating, drinking, or loud phone calls on the sacred paths.
visitGuide.gettingThere: JR Harajuku Station or Metro Meiji-jingumae. Follow signs into the forested approach.
visitGuide.bestTime: Early morning for quiet. Weekends and New Year are extremely busy. Autumn foliage is beautiful.
notes: Photography is usually fine outdoors; respect signs near the main sanctuary.
Wedding processions are common — give them space.

name: Tōdai-ji
summary: Home of the Great Buddha of Nara — one of Japan’s most monumental wooden halls, set among free-roaming deer.

practical.tickets: Separate tickets for Daibutsuden (Great Buddha Hall) and some sub-temples.
practical.dress: Casual modest dress is fine. Remove hats indoors.

etiquette: Speak quietly inside the Great Buddha Hall.
Do not feed deer human junk food; use official crackers if you choose to feed them.
Watch belongings — deer will nuzzle bags.
visitGuide.gettingThere: JR or Kintetsu Nara Station, then 20–30 minutes on foot through Nara Park, or a short bus ride.
visitGuide.bestTime: Weekday mornings. Cherry blossom and autumn colour seasons are peak.
notes: The hall is a reconstruction (18th century) of an earlier, even larger structure.
Combine with Kasuga Taisha and Kōfuku-ji for a full Nara day.

name: Wat Arun
summary: The Temple of Dawn — a porcelain-encrusted prang on the Chao Phraya, glowing at sunrise and after dark.

practical.hours: Typically morning to early evening — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Modest entry fee for the grounds; river ferry is separate.
practical.dress: Cover shoulders and knees. Sarongs often available to rent or buy at the gate.

etiquette: Climb carefully — stairs are steep and narrow.
Do not point feet at Buddha images.
Remove shoes where indicated.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Cross the Chao Phraya by ferry from Tha Tien (near Wat Pho). River boats and taxis also serve the west bank.
visitGuide.bestTime: Late afternoon into dusk for soft light on the prang; sunrise lives up to the name if you start early.
notes: Combine with Wat Pho and the Grand Palace across the river.
Verify before visit: upper-terrace access may close for conservation.

name: Wat Phra Kaew
summary: Thailand’s most sacred Buddhist temple, within the Grand Palace complex, home to the Emerald Buddha.

practical.hours: Usually daytime only; last entry earlier than closing — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Combined Grand Palace ticket; keep your ticket for museum sections.
practical.dress: Strict: covered shoulders, long trousers or skirts covering knees, closed or neat sandals. No torn clothing.
practical.duration: 2–3 hours for palace and temple grounds.

etiquette: No photography inside the ordination hall of the Emerald Buddha.
Speak quietly; this is an active royal and religious site.
Sit with feet tucked away from the Buddha image.
visitGuide.gettingThere: BTS to Saphan Taksin then river boat, or MRT + taxi/tuk-tuk to the Grand Palace. Arrive early to avoid peak queues.
visitGuide.bestTime: Open immediately at opening time on a weekday. Avoid major royal ceremonies when access may shift.
notes: Dress-code checks are real — bring a scarf or light trousers.
Verify before visit: schedules change around royal and national events.

name: Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple)
summary: The holiest gurdwara of Sikhism — a gold-clad sanctuary in a sacred pool, open to all who come with respect.

practical.hours: Open virtually around the clock for devotees; visitor patterns peak morning and evening — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Free entry. Donations welcome. Langar (community kitchen) is free to all.
practical.dress: Cover your head (scarves provided). Remove shoes. Wash feet at the entrance pools. Modest clothing.

etiquette: Head covering is mandatory for everyone.
No alcohol, tobacco, or intoxicants on the complex.
Photography rules vary by zone — follow signs and sewadars’ guidance.
Sit on the floor in langar; accept food respectfully.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Amritsar airport or railway station, then auto-rickshaw or taxi to the walled old city. Expect security screening.
visitGuide.bestTime: Early morning or late evening for golden light on the sarovar. Major gurpurabs are deeply moving but extremely crowded.
notes: Security is thorough — travel light.
The experience is spiritual first, touristic second — move with humility.

name: Potala Palace
summary: The iconic hilltop palace-monastery of Lhasa — white and red walls above the city, a landmark of Tibetan Buddhism.

quickFacts.unesco: Historic Ensemble of the Potala Palace (1994)

practical.hours: Daytime timed tickets; daily visitor caps apply — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Advance booking is typically essential in peak season. Bring passport.
practical.dress: Modest layers. Lhasa is high altitude — prepare for sun and chill.
practical.duration: About 1 hour inside once entered; allow more for the climb and security.

etiquette: Follow one-way routes; do not touch murals or statues.
Speak quietly in chapels.
Photography is restricted or banned in many rooms — obey signs.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Fly into Lhasa (LXA) with required permits for many foreign visitors. Local guides and operators handle logistics — confirm current entry rules.
visitGuide.bestTime: May–October for milder weather. Acclimatise to altitude before intensive sightseeing.
notes: Altitude sickness is real — rest on arrival day.
Verify before visit: ticket systems and permit rules change frequently.
Pair with Jokhang Temple and Barkhor for context.

name: Po Lin Monastery & Tian Tan Buddha
summary: Hong Kong’s hillside monastery and the monumental Big Buddha — reached by cable car over green islands and sea.

practical.hours: Monastery and Buddha viewing generally daytime; cable car hours vary — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Ngong Ping 360 cable car tickets; monastery grounds typically free; museum/Buddha podium may have fees.
practical.dress: Modest clothing for monastery halls. Comfortable shoes for stairs to the Buddha.

etiquette: Remove shoes where posted in temple halls.
Keep voices low; this remains an active monastery.
Do not climb on statues or offerings.
visitGuide.gettingThere: MTR to Tung Chung, then Ngong Ping 360 cable car or bus. Allow buffer for cable-car queues and weather delays.
visitGuide.bestTime: Weekday mornings. Clear days for views; fog is common and atmospheric but hides the skyline.
notes: Vegetarian meals are available near the monastery.
Combine with Tai O fishing village if time allows.

name: Dome of the Rock & Al-Aqsa Compound
summary: One of Islam’s holiest sites — the golden Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa Mosque on the Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount plateau. Visit with care and current access rules.

practical.hours: Non-Muslim visiting hours are limited and change often — verify before visit with official sources on the day.
practical.tickets: Entry rules differ for worshippers and visitors; expect security checks. Bring passport.
practical.dress: Very modest: covered arms and legs; women may need a headscarf. Shoes off in prayer spaces if entered.

etiquette: This is an active sacred site for Muslims — behave with utmost respect.
Follow police and Waqf instructions without argument.
Do not bring religious artefacts of other faiths onto the compound.
Photography rules can be strict — ask if unsure.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Access points in Jerusalem’s Old City are controlled. Queues form early on open days.
visitGuide.bestTime: Only when official visiting windows are open. Avoid prayer rush times as a tourist.
notes: Access for non-Muslims is frequently adjusted for security and religious calendar — always verify same-day.
SanctaWay presents factual visit guidance only; the site’s religious and political significance deserves humility.
Interior access to the Dome and Al-Aqsa is often reserved for Muslim worshippers.

name: Hagia Sophia
summary: Justinian’s 6th-century great church, later mosque, museum, and mosque again — a hinge of Byzantine and Ottoman sacred architecture.

practical.hours: Open as a mosque with visitor windows outside prayer times — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Entry arrangements have changed with status; check the current official ticket or free-entry policy.
practical.dress: Mosque dress code: covered shoulders and knees; women should cover hair. Shoes off on carpeted areas.

etiquette: Remain quiet during prayer.
Stay on visitor paths; do not enter restricted prayer zones when asked.
No flash photography toward worshippers.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Tram T1 to Sultanahmet. The building faces the Hippodrome and Blue Mosque.
visitGuide.bestTime: Weekday mornings between prayer times. Pair with the Blue Mosque and Topkapı for a Sultanahmet day.
notes: Status and visitor rules have changed in recent years — verify same-week guidance.
Upper galleries may have separate access or closures.

name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
summary: Christianity’s most venerated church — traditionally the sites of the Crucifixion and the Tomb, shared by several denominations.

practical.hours: Long daily hours; last entry for the Tomb queue can close earlier — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Free entry. Expect queues for the Aedicule (Tomb).
practical.dress: Modest clothing covering shoulders and knees. Remove hats in some chapels.
practical.duration: 1–2 hours; longer if waiting for the Tomb.

etiquette: This is an active place of pilgrimage — keep voices low.
Do not push in processions or candle lines.
Photography is generally allowed but avoid flash on icons and during liturgy.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Christian Quarter of Jerusalem’s Old City. Multiple gates; follow pilgrim signage.
visitGuide.bestTime: Early morning on weekdays. Holy Week and Orthodox Easter are profound but intensely crowded.
notes: Different chapels belong to different communities — follow local caretakers’ directions.
Stone of Anointing near the entrance is a focus of devotion — be patient.

name: Sagrada Família
summary: Gaudí’s unfinished basilica — stone forests of light, still rising after more than a century of work.

practical.hours: Long daytime hours; last entry ~30–60 minutes before close — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Timed-entry tickets are essential; buy only from the official website. Tower tickets are separate.
practical.dress: Shoulders and thighs covered for basilica entry.

etiquette: This is a functioning church — keep voices respectful.
No large bags; security screening applies.
Follow stewards during Mass times.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Metro L2/L5 Sagrada Família. Arrive 15 minutes before your timed slot.
visitGuide.bestTime: Morning for softer façade light; late afternoon for warmer interior colour through the stained glass.
notes: Construction continues — some façades and towers may be scaffolded.
Audio guides are excellent for first visits.

name: Notre-Dame de Paris
summary: The Gothic heart of Paris on the Île de la Cité — restored and reopened after the 2019 fire, with ongoing works to note.

practical.hours: Reopening schedules and reservation systems evolve — verify before visit on the official cathedral site.
practical.tickets: Nave entry policies may include free entry with timed reservation; towers/treasury may differ.
practical.dress: Modest attire appropriate for a cathedral.

etiquette: Silence phones; speak softly.
Do not obstruct liturgy or prayer areas.
Follow stewards around restored and restricted zones.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Cité or Saint-Michel Métro; walk onto Île de la Cité. Security queues are common.
visitGuide.bestTime: Weekday mornings. Evening exterior views from the Left Bank are classic.
notes: Status note: post-2019 restoration reopened the cathedral to worship and visitors; some exterior and related works may continue — verify current access.
Book ahead if reservations are required.

name: St. Peter’s Basilica
summary: The great basilica of Catholicism — Michelangelo’s dome over the alleged tomb of Saint Peter, facing the colonnades of Bernini.

practical.hours: Morning to late afternoon typically; closes during major papal events — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Basilica entry is generally free; cupola climb and sacristy/treasury have fees. Security is airport-style.
practical.dress: Strict: no bare shoulders or knees. Shawls help. No hats for men inside.

etiquette: Maintain silence near chapels and the Baldachin.
Kneeling and prayer take priority over photos.
No drones; follow Swiss Guard and security directions.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Metro Ottaviano or Cipro, then walk. Combine carefully with Vatican Museums (separate tickets, long queues).
visitGuide.bestTime: Early weekday morning. Papal audiences and major feast days transform access.
notes: Climb the dome for the classic Rome view — steep stairs at the end.
Verify before visit around Easter, Christmas, and conclave-related periods.

name: Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe
summary: The most visited Marian shrine in the world — old and new basilicas beneath Tepeyac hill, centre of Guadalupe devotion.

practical.hours: Long daily hours for pilgrims — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Free entry to the basilicas. Museum sections may charge.
practical.dress: Modest clothing. Expect large pilgrim crowds.
practical.duration: 2–3 hours for both basilicas and plaza.

etiquette: This is a living pilgrimage site — move patiently.
Do not block the moving walkway under the tilma display.
Ask before photographing individuals at prayer.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Mexico City Metro La Villa-Basílica. The complex is well signed from the station.
visitGuide.bestTime: Weekday mornings. 12 December (feast day) is extraordinary and extremely crowded.
notes: Visit both the modern circular basilica and the historic church on the hill.
Vendors and pilgrim stalls surround the plaza — keep valuables secure.

name: Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
summary: A constellation of medieval churches carved from living rock — Ethiopia’s ‘New Jerusalem’ still in active Orthodox use.

practical.hours: Daytime access for visitors; liturgy schedules differ — verify before visit.
practical.tickets: Multi-day visitor tickets sold locally; hire a licensed guide for context and navigation.
practical.dress: Cover shoulders and knees. Women often cover hair in churches. Remove shoes at thresholds.
practical.duration: One full day for both clusters of churches.

etiquette: Remove shoes before entering each church.
Ask before photographing priests, pilgrims, or interiors.
Step carefully — rock paths can be uneven and steep.
visitGuide.gettingThere: Fly into Lalibela (LLI) from Addis Ababa. Town is walkable between church clusters with a guide.
visitGuide.bestTime: Dry season (roughly October–March). Timkat (Epiphany) is spectacular and crowded.
notes: Altitude and sun are strong — pace yourself and hydrate.
Some protective shelters cover churches — they alter photos but protect the stone.
Verify before visit: ticket prices and photography rules change.
